item.title: Dear Graduates: Reflections on the AI Workplace
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Dear Graduates: Reflections on the AI Workplace

A note to the class of 2026 and all who love them, live with them, or employ them.

Posted June 22, 2026

Key points
  • The World Economic Forum projects AI will cut 92 million jobs by 2030 but create 170 million new ones.
  • LinkedIn ranked AI engineer the fastest-growing U.S. job title in 2026, with postings up 143% year over year.
  • Research links meaningful work to higher life satisfaction, better mental health, and even longer life.

The average American adult will spend roughly 80,000 to 90,000 hours at work over a lifetime. That is about a third of their waking life. That number comes from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, and it's worth sitting with as you reflect on what to do next.

Last weekend, I sat at my alma mater's psychology graduation, watching thousands of young people cross the stage 43 years after I did the same. While the similarities were obvious, the world they are entering is radically different than the one I stepped into. These are the first generation to enter a workforce being rapidly reshaped by AI, with a future harder than ever to predict.

Their Next Steps

Work isn't just about a paycheck and creating independence from your family of origin. It is so much more. It supplies structure, identity, and community, which profoundly shape one’s adulthood. People who find genuine meaning in their work report higher life satisfaction, better mental health, stronger relationships, and even longer lives. People stuck in work that feels pointless or misaligned with their values face a measurably higher risk of depression, anxiety, and burnout.

So the question graduates face isn't only "What job can I get?" It should be, "What work will let me become the best version of myself and motivate me to keep growing?"

Meaningful work rarely arrives gift-wrapped. More often, it's built and rebuilt over time with considerable effort and bravery. People who actively look for ways to connect their daily tasks to something larger are far more likely to find that connection. Researchers call this job crafting: reshaping a role, even incrementally, to better fit your values and strengths. It's something workers have more control over than they tend to assume. As we grow and change, so do our interests, and the most fortunate are the ones who give themselves opportunities to try new things along the way.

What the Data Actually Says About AI and Jobs

It is reasonable to be anxious about entering the labor market at this unique time, but there is good news, despite what the gloom and doom headlines may suggest. The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 projects that by 2030, AI and related shifts will displace roughly 92 million jobs globally while creating 170 million new ones, a net gain of 78 million positions. While the unsettling first number grabs our attention, the second one should inform our decision-making. The fastest-growing roles either work with AI directly or rely on distinctly human capacities AI can't replicate.

Here are a few tips to guide you:

  • Technology and AI-adjacent fields are growing fastest of all, which is not a surprise. LinkedIn's 2026 Jobs on the Rise report ranked AI engineer the No. 1 fastest-growing job title in the U.S., with postings up 143% year over year, and four of the top five fastest-growing titles overall were AI-related. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics separately projects computer and mathematical occupations to grow more than three times faster than the economy as a whole, driven in part by demand for AI development and data analysis.

  • Healthcare and mental healthcare remain powerhouses. BLS projects that the employment of substance abuse, behavioral disorder, and mental health counselors will grow 16.8% through 2034, clinical and counseling psychologists 11.2%, and mental health and substance abuse social workers 9.7%. AI can flag a risk pattern or summarize a session note. It cannot sit with a frightened patient, hold someone's hand through a diagnosis, or do the relational work that therapy actually is. The demand for human presence in healing is universal, and the health field faces a persistent shortage of providers relative to the need.

  • Your humanity still matters. Education, skilled trades, creative direction, legal services, and social entrepreneurship all share a common thread: human judgment, empathy, and creative problem-solving stay central to the work. AI is changing how these jobs get done, but it is largely assisting rather than replacing, which is freeing people for the more complex, relational parts of the role.

article continues after advertisement

Where the Headwinds Are

Some fields are genuinely more exposed. Routine data entry, basic customer service, repetitive legal and accounting tasks, entry-level writing and coding work, and certain manufacturing roles are all seeing real automation pressure. That doesn't mean these fields are vanishing. It does mean the people who thrive within them will be the ones who build the higher-level, human-centered skills the work still requires, rather than the narrowly repetitive tasks a model can already do faster.

The most useful framing I can offer: Learn to work alongside AI rather than in competition with it. Treat it as a powerful tool rather than a rival. Those most likely to thrive in an AI workforce will be the ones who use it to extend what they're already good at doing.

Points to Ponder

Don't chase prestige at the expense of meaning. I've sat across from many accomplished, outwardly "successful" people who are unhappy because they chose a career for status or income rather than meaning. Money matters, but research consistently finds that beyond a comfortable income, additional earnings add surprisingly little to day-to-day happiness. What does add to happiness is autonomy, mastery, and a genuine sense that your work matters.

You're allowed to not have it figured out. Our 20s have aptly been called “the defining decade” by psychologist Meg Jay. Some of the most fulfilled people build their careers only after wandering through several false starts first. What looks like a detour often turns out to be foundational. I spent 19 years in academic medicine before 16 more years in private practice as a psychiatrist. Along the way, I found some of my most meaningful work in places I hadn't trained for at all, including writing and nonprofit work inspired by raising a daughter with cerebral palsy.

Stay curious. The shelf life of any specific skill is shrinking fast. What predicts long-term success isn't how much someone knows on graduation day. This is just the start. The key is to keep asking questions and keep learning. That habit, more than any single credential, is what will carry this generation through the next 45 years in the workforce.

You are entering a complicated, fast-moving world. You are also entering a world with more possibilities than ever before. I am wishing you all the best as you begin your transition to the next phase of life.

item.title: Rain at the Acropolis: When Imperfection Makes Stronger Memories
item.description:
Memory

Rain at the Acropolis: When Imperfection Makes Stronger Memories

Why some of our most meaningful memories emerge when life doesn't go to plan.

Posted June 22, 2026

Key points
  • Some of our most cherished memories emerge from imperfect circumstances.
  • Psychological flexibility helps us transform unexpected challenges into meaningful experiences.
  • Small acts of adaptation today may strengthen our ability to navigate larger challenges tomorrow.

When we imagine Greece, we easily picture blue skies and warm sunshine. As a faculty member who has led a study abroad program in Greece for years, I carried those same expectations with me when we visited this summer. However, that was not our experience this summer. When our group made its way toward the Acropolis, dark clouds gathered overhead. Before long, rain began to fall. Many of us had not brought umbrellas or rain jackets, the marble pathways became slick under our feet, phone cameras disappeared into pockets, and our shoes were quickly soaked.

As the rain continued, the postcard-perfect scenes we had envisioned seemed increasingly unlikely. As the faculty leader, I was initially disappointed because I worried that my students would feel they were missing out on the experience they had anticipated. They had traveled thousands of miles to visit the Acropolis, one of the most famous historical landmarks in the world, and rain was certainly not part of the plan.

Finding Meaning in Unexpected Moments

Yet something unexpected happened. Students shared umbrellas, took photos anyway, and helped one another make their way down the slippery marble pathways. I joked that perhaps we were all lucky to be at the Acropolis in the rain, as this was my first time experiencing rain at the Acropolis. Everyone laughed instead of complaining. Some even remarked that the rain made their experience unforgettable. As I watched the group, I found myself reflecting on a question that extends far beyond travel: Why do some of our most meaningful memories emerge when life doesn’t go according to plan?

Many of us spend our lives pursuing perfect experiences. We carefully plan trips, celebrations, careers, and even assignment deadlines, and hope that everything will unfold according to plan. We often assume that the closer an experience comes to perfection, the more meaningful it will be. Yet, our brains naturally tend to remember unexpected experiences more vividly than routine (Kafkas et al., 2025). Some of our most cherished memories arise from moments that were unplanned. The rain at the Acropolis transformed our visit into a story. Years from now, my students may not remember every moment we shared in Greece. However, many of them will remember standing together atop the Acropolis, sharing umbrellas, and taking photos in the rain.

How Shared Challenges Strengthen Group Bonds

The experience also reminded me of something I have observed repeatedly when traveling with students: shared challenges often bring us together. Research supports this observation, indicating that shared discomfort can strengthen feelings of connection and belonging (Bastian et al., 2014). The rain created a small but meaningful challenge that everyone experienced together. We shared umbrellas, laughed at the unusual weather, and helped one another navigate the slippery walk down. The rain had brought us a little closer together.

article continues after advertisement

This experience extends beyond the study abroad program. As many of us have experienced, life does not always unfold according to plan. Some of our most meaningful opportunities emerge from places we never anticipated. What matters is not whether circumstances change, but how we respond. Psychologists refer to this capacity as psychological flexibility, the ability to adjust our thoughts and behaviors in response to changing circumstances. Research has linked psychological flexibility to psychological health, emotional well-being, and improved well-being (Kashdan, & Rottenberg, 2010). What we experienced together at the Acropolis in the rain exemplified this. The day was far from perfect, yet it became a moment that we will always cherish as an unforgettable and meaningful memory.

item.title: Why I Use ACT in Pregnancy and Postpartum Therapy
item.description:
Postpartum Depression

Why I Use ACT in Pregnancy and Postpartum Therapy

Therapy helps moms navigate anxiety, uncertainty, and overwhelm differently.

Posted June 22, 2026

Key points
  • ACT focuses on changing your relationship to thoughts and emotions.
  • Pregnancy and postpartum often involve uncertainty that cannot be fully controlled.
  • Psychological flexibility is strongly linked to emotional resilience in motherhood.
  • ACT helps mothers stay connected to their values even during difficult moments.

Acceptance and commitment therapy helps mothers navigate anxiety, uncertainty, and overwhelm with greater flexibility and self-compassion.

When women reach out for therapy during pregnancy or after the birth of a child, they are often exhausted. Some are consumed by anxiety that seems impossible to quiet. Others are struggling with intrusive thoughts, grief, perfectionism, panic, or the relentless feeling that they are somehow falling short. Almost all of them want relief, and understandably so.

Relief matters. But one of the things I often explain early in treatment is that my goal is not simply to help someone get rid of uncomfortable thoughts and feelings. While symptom reduction is certainly important, my experience has been that motherhood does not always cooperate with our desire to feel calm, certain, and in control. Pregnancy and postpartum are periods of tremendous change, and much of that change unfolds beyond our ability to predict or manage perfectly.

This is one of the reasons I am drawn to acceptance and commitment therapy. Although ACT can be applied to many concerns, I have found it particularly helpful for women navigating pregnancy and early motherhood because it acknowledges something many mothers already know deep down: Uncertainty is unavoidable.

There are the obvious uncertainties—the health of a pregnancy, labor and delivery, feeding decisions, sleep, and returning to work. But there are also deeper uncertainties. Will I be a good mother? Will I lose myself? Why don't I feel the way I thought I would? What if something happens to my baby? These questions can be deeply painful, and no amount of reassurance can eliminate them.

In response, many women understandably begin working harder. They spend hours researching. They compare themselves to other mothers. They seek reassurance from friends, family, social media, or Google. Some become increasingly self-critical, convinced that if they could just think differently, prepare more thoroughly, or stop feeling anxious, they would finally feel better.

What I have observed, however, is that much of the suffering women experience comes not from the presence of difficult thoughts and emotions themselves, but from becoming locked in a struggle against them. The battle to eliminate uncertainty often becomes exhausting. Ironically, the harder we fight anxiety, the more our lives begin to revolve around it.

At the heart of ACT is the concept of psychological flexibility—the ability to remain present and respond intentionally, even when fear, sadness, guilt, or self-doubt are present. Rather than waiting to feel better before engaging life, psychological flexibility allows us to continue moving toward what matters, even while carrying difficult emotions.

This is especially important because parenting rarely unfolds according to plan. I have yet to meet a mother who feels confident and joyful all the time. Some of the most devoted and loving mothers I know are also deeply anxious, highly sensitive, or prone to self-doubt. The presence of these experiences does not mean they are broken. More often, it reflects that they care deeply.

article continues after advertisement

Many mothers are surprised to hear that emotional pain does not necessarily indicate pathology. Sometimes distress makes sense in context. Caring for a newborn while sleeping in fragmented stretches, recovering physically, adjusting to a new identity, and carrying enormous responsibility is hard. Grieving a miscarriage or navigating infertility is hard. Parenting after trauma is hard. Feeling overwhelmed by these experiences does not mean something is wrong with you. It means you are human.

One ACT process I use frequently is cognitive defusion, which involves learning to step back and observe thoughts rather than immediately treating them as facts. Mothers often tell me, "I'm failing." "My baby deserves a better mother." "I should be handling this better." They frequently assume these thoughts are evidence of some deeper truth.

But thoughts are not verdicts. They are mental events.

Learning to say, "I'm having the thought that I'm failing," may seem like a subtle shift, but it creates space. Suddenly, a thought that felt absolute becomes something that can be noticed rather than obeyed. Painful thoughts don't disappear, but it can loosen their grip.

I am also drawn to ACT because it makes room for emotional complexity. Motherhood has a way of bringing contradictory feelings to the surface, and many women judge themselves harshly for this. They assume that loving their child should eliminate loneliness, resentment, grief, or sadness. Yet human beings are capable of holding more than one truth at a time.

A mother can adore her baby and miss her old life. She can feel grateful for a pregnancy and terrified by the changes it brings. She can experience immense joy while simultaneously mourning a previous miscarriage or wondering whether she will ever feel like herself again. These emotional contradictions are part of being human, not evidence of failure.

ACT also helps shift attention away from perfection and back toward values. These may not be the right questions: "Am I doing this right?" "Why can't I handle this better?" Instead, we begin asking different questions. How do I want to show up? What kind of mother do I hope to be? What qualities do I want to embody, even when things are difficult?

I often remind mothers that values are directions, not destinations. Being a loving parent does not require feeling loving every moment, nor does it mean never feeling frustrated. A mother can feel anxious and still act with compassion. She can feel overwhelmed and still choose presence. She can have intrusive thoughts and still be an excellent parent.

article continues after advertisement

People sometimes misunderstand acceptance and assume it means giving up or settling. In reality, acceptance involves acknowledging reality rather than exhausting ourselves by arguing with it. Acceptance might sound like, "This is hard right now." Or, "I wish things were different." It might mean acknowledging anxiety without demanding certainty or recognizing grief without trying to rush it away.

Interestingly, many women discover that when they stop waging war against their inner experience, they become less consumed by it. Not because the feelings disappear, but because they are no longer spending all of their energy trying to escape them.

Healing rarely happens through one dramatic breakthrough. More often, it unfolds through countless small moments of flexibility, courage, self-compassion, and support.

One of the things I tell mothers most often is that the presence of anxiety, intrusive thoughts, grief, overwhelm, or emotional pain does not mean they are doing motherhood wrong. It means they are navigating one of the most demanding and transformative experiences life can bring.

And perhaps most importantly, it means they do not have to navigate it alone.

item.title: Learning to Share
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

Learning to Share

Personal Perspective: How should I respond when critters eat my plants?

Posted June 22, 2026

Key points
  • Gardens attract all sorts of critters, and some will eat the plants.
  • Being realistic about what one is prepared to let go of helps avoid feeling deprived or resentful.
  • Sometimes simple boundaries like fences or wire cages make a large difference.
My daisies.
Source: Annita Sawyer

The clump of daisies stands round and tall. Its green leaves shine and shimmer in the breeze. Small but swelling buds—white buttons rimmed with green—top each stem. They’re almost ready to bloom. Thrilling with anticipation, I imagine the cloud of happy flowers: my daisies will delight me.

At the same time, I’m trying to prepare myself to let them go. Fuzz Face the woodchuck who lives under the shed might eat them. One day last summer I saw that all of the daisies were blooming. The next morning, every blossom was gone. They’d grown tall enough that only a large animal could have reached them.

Now the daisies are back, making a clump even larger than before. Their buds grow fatter every day. I checked this morning and again this afternoon to see if they’d popped. Not yet.

I refer to Fuzz Face as "he," but in fact I have no idea if the woodchuck this year is a "he" or a "she," and I don’t know if he’s the same one from last year. In fact, the woodchuck I saw yesterday looked smaller than I thought the one last week appeared. It may be a whole family. A few years ago, we often saw two small woodchucks in the yard—two babies—along with a large adult. They were really cute. But of course they would grow up, and along the way they and their parents would eat our plants.

This year’s Fuzz Face feasts on a lawn dense with clover, all kinds of grass, and weeds of every sort. I’m glad that he likes what’s on offer and spends most of his time just munching through it. I enjoy watching him—our own local wildlife representative. I was also disappointed—OK, mad—when I saw him eating the new shoots of the red cone flower I’d bought at the farmers market last summer.

After a bitter cold winter, I was delighted to see tiny cone flower shoots appear this spring. Not long ago they’d grown small leaves; a day after that, just a half-inch of stalk remained. Then again they’d grow larger, and again they’d get eaten. A few days ago, I looked out the glass patio doors and saw Fuzz Face in the process of eating more leaves. I stifled my first impulse to rush out yelling and waving my hands to scare him away—I did that last year, thinking I’d teach him a lesson. This time, I thought about my plan to share.

It’s easy to be high-minded in the abstract. Of course I want to share all the goodness around me. There’s nothing I’m growing that I can’t do without. But picturing lost flowers or vegetables eaten by critters, a disappointed voice yells, It’s mine, I planted it, I wanted it, hands off—it’s mine!

Coreopsis seedlings under wire.
Source: Annita Sawyer

A while later, I saw Fuzz Face eating the longest leaves of two Coreopsis Early Sunrise seedlings Will and I had planted the day before. I’d been savoring the prospect of bright clumps of the double-petaled sunny yellow flowers their labels promised. At that moment I reconsidered my attitude about sharing with the critters. Using the wire we’d purchased last year to make a fence around the peach tree, I set up a protective barrier for both the coreopsis seedlings and the cone flower. In my mind it was a compromise between giving freely and protecting my plants.

article continues after advertisement

As of today, they’re still OK—diminished from their original growth, but not subsequently disturbed. I’m assuming that there’s enough of the leaves left for them to grow into full flowering plants. I’ve accepted the idea that critters will continue to nibble the zinnias. A few hours ago, I checked the new summer squash and zucchini plants. Rabbits might already have eaten some blossoms.

Yellow squash and zucchini.
Source: Annita Sawyer

Can I truly make peace with the woodchucks and the rabbits and the chipmunks and who knows what else who need to feed themselves and their babies? There’s no reason why they shouldn’t eat what they like if it’s right there. It was easier to be mellow after a friend helped us add underground wire fencing around the edge of the big garden where we grow the vegetables, herbs, and large dahlias. I thought it kept the big critters out. Today I discovered a dug up dahlia tuber—the first time the dahlias have ever been disturbed.

I Googled methods of controlling garden critters. In addition to various sprays and potions, I discovered sonic devices—some solar, some battery powered—used to repel them. These machines generate sound waves that torment the various animals, making their lives so miserable that they move away. They find new places to dig their tunnels and raise their pups.

Forcing Fuzz Face to go elsewhere by hounding him with noise feels deeply wrong. It’s cruel; I don’t want to do that. I’m even more determined to share.

When I’m feeling fulfilled and grateful to be alive, I tell myself life’s too short to spend time being upset. I don’t want to resent a fellow mammal who’s hungry and only wants to eat what looks best. It’s less about what I’m losing and more about just being kind.

Live and let live holds profound implications for me in my 80s, when not one day can be taken for granted.
